title: Read web addresses properly
intro: A short explainer video with two questions along the way.
transfer: This week, read the address bar at every login: which domain comes right before the ending?

scenes.caption: A web address has parts. What counts is the domain: the part right before the ending.
Here the page belongs to “account-check.example”. The “samplebank” in front is only a subdomain that anyone can create.
A padlock symbol does not protect you from fraud either. It only shows that the connection is encrypted, not who owns the page.

questions.explanation: What counts is the part right before the ending: “account-check.example”.

questions.prompt: What does the padlock symbol in the address bar tell you?
options: The page surely belongs to the bank
The page was checked by the government
The connection to the page is encrypted
questions.explanation: The padlock only shows the encrypted connection. Fraudsters have padlocks too.

title: Account locked?
intro: Tap everything that makes you suspicious, in the email and on the website behind it. Then decide: phishing or genuine?
transfer: With the next email that has a link, check before you click: the sender's domain and the link target.

content.disclaimer: Practice example with the made-up brand “Samplebank” and reserved example addresses (.example). Nothing is real, nothing is sent. The real address of the made-up bank would be samplebank.example.

signal.explanation: The domain is “samplebank-support.example”, not “samplebank.example”. Anyone can choose any display name.

mail.text: URGENT: Your account will be locked in 24 hours

signal.explanation: Time pressure and threats are meant to stop you from checking.
Your bank knows your name. An impersonal greeting is a warning sign.

mail.text: we have detected unusual activity in your account. Please confirm your identity.
mail.harmless: Not a strong sign on its own: real security emails sound similar.

signal.explanation: The link goes to “account-check.example”. “samplebank” is only at the front as camouflage.

mail.harmless: A signature can be copied freely.

signal.explanation: What counts is the part before the ending: “account-check.example”. That is not the bank.

site.harmless: The heading alone is not a clue.

site.text: Contract number · Password · Card number · Security code (CVC)

signal.explanation: Password and full card details together, through a link from an email: no bank asks for that.

site.harmless: The button is disabled here and is not a clue on its own.

content.verdictExplanation: Several strong clues together: a foreign domain for the sender and the website, time pressure and a request for password and card details.

title: Only a CHF 1.95 fee?
intro: A small amount, a well-known brand. Tap everything suspicious and decide.
transfer: With payment requests by email or text message: never pay through the link; enter the tracking number yourself on the site you know.

content.disclaimer: Practice example with the made-up brand “Sample Parcel Post” and addresses on .example. The real address of the made-up post would be sample-parcelpost.example.

mail.text: Your parcel is waiting: customs fee due
mail.harmless: The subject sounds normal. That is exactly what makes this scam work.
A rather weak sign; many real shipping emails greet you without a name.

mail.text: a fee of CHF 1.95 is due for your parcel. Without payment, the parcel will be returned to the sender.
mail.harmless: A small amount is meant to make checking seem unnecessary. On its own, though, not a sure sign.

signal.explanation: The link goes to “payment-info.example”, not to the post.

site.harmless: The heading alone is not a clue.

site.text: Card number · Expiry date · Security code (CVC) · Name

signal.explanation: Full card details for CHF 1.95: afterwards a much larger amount is often charged.

content.verdictExplanation: A foreign domain for the sender, link and website, and a request for full card details. The small amount is the bait.

title: Real or not?
intro: Not every email is phishing. Check carefully and mark only what is really suspicious.
transfer: If you requested something yourself and the sender and link match the known domain, the email is probably genuine. If in doubt, open the site yourself.

content.disclaimer: Practice example with the made-up company “Samplebank” and addresses on .example. Two minutes ago you requested a new password yourself.

mail.harmless: The domain is “samplebank.example”, the bank's real address.

mail.text: Your link to reset your password
mail.harmless: Matches your request from two minutes ago.
A personal greeting with your name.

mail.text: You requested a new password. The link is valid for 30 minutes. If this wasn't you, ignore this email.
mail.harmless: The time limit is normal for such links, and there is a way out without pressure.
The link goes to the real domain “samplebank.example”.

site.harmless: Not a clue on its own.
Only a new password is requested, no card details.

content.verdictExplanation: Sender, link and website belong to the real domain, the email matches your own request and asks for no sensitive data.
